strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in joint speech-text modeling: the much longer sequence length of conventional speech tokens. Using ASR decoder queries to produce transcription-length speech representations is intuitive and potentially useful.

TASTE combines reconstruction-trained, text-aligned representations with both discrete RVQ and continuous-embedding language-modeling variants. The word-level mechanism for reconciling ASR and LLM tokenizers is practically motivated.

The reported results provide a promising empirical signal: TASTE achieves 3.8% WER, 4.25 UTMOS, and 0.84 speaker similarity at roughly 190 bit/s, while both TASLM variants substantially outperform the authors' S3-token LoRA baseline on SALMON and StoryCloze.
The evaluation considers intelligibility, naturalness, speaker, emotion, duration, acoustic modeling, and semantic modeling. The main architecture and model choices are presented relatively clearly.
weaknesses: The central claim of an effective spoken language model is insufficiently evaluated. Reconstruction uses speech features extracted from the target utterance, while SALMON and StoryCloze are likelihood-ranking tasks; there is no evaluation of speech generated from TASLM-predicted tokens or embeddings, no human listening study, and no assessment of generated continuation intelligibility, naturalness, semantics, or diversity.

The evidence isolating text alignment is weak. The only controlled downstream baseline, S3-token LoRA, is near chance on several tasks. Comparisons with prior systems use different data, architectures, model sizes, and training procedures. Missing controls include matched full fine-tuning, length- or bitrate-matched tokens, simple pooling/downsampling, forced alignment, and ablations of ASR initialization, shallow-value cross-attention, word averaging, and RVQ design.

The reconstruction comparison is not information-rate-equivalent: TASTE additionally conditions its decoder on the transcript and a target speaker embedding, whereas some codec baselines do not, and the reported bitrate excludes these side channels. UTMOS exceeding the ground-truth score illustrates why this estimator cannot substitute for human evaluation. Confidence intervals, significance tests, and complete definitions of speaker, emotion, and duration metrics are also absent.

Claims of dramatic computational savings are unsupported by measurements. The paper reports neither token-rate distributions nor context lengths, FLOPs, memory, throughput, latency, or matched training/inference cost. Robustness to ASR errors, noise, accents, domains, and languages is likewise untested despite the tokenizer requiring a transcript.

Important technical details are ambiguous or inconsistent. Algorithm 1 returns only an averaged embedding although the text also claims aligned discrete indices; the placement of averaging and requantization is unclear. The fusion and autoregressive inference procedure for the text and speech streams is unspecified. The embedding objective omits the text prediction loss despite claiming joint output, while the KL target, straight-through estimator, RVQ gradients, and loss weighting are inadequately defined.

Reproducibility is limited: the paper does not clearly state which datasets train each stage, the SLM training duration or number of updates, loss coefficients, LoRA target modules, likelihood normalization, decoding settings, random seeds, or run variance, and it provides no code, checkpoints, or audio samples. The stated five epochs over approximately 40,600 hours in two days on eight A6000 GPUs also require clarification.

There is no discussion of consent, privacy, demographic bias, impersonation, or misuse despite training on large-scale web speech and enabling speaker-conditioned speech generation. Overall, the idea is promising, but the missing controlled experiments and direct generation evidence are major rather than marginal deficiencies for a top-tier venue.

The reported compression-quality tradeoff is promising. TASTE obtains 3.8% WER, 4.25 UTMOS, and competitive emotion, duration, and speaker consistency at approximately 190 bit/s, roughly ten times below the comparable four-layer SpeechTokenizer configuration.

Several comparisons are confounded. The claimed computational savings are not supported by latency, memory, FLOP, throughput, or trainable-parameter measurements.

Important methodological details are missing or inconsistent enough to limit reproducibility. Algorithm 1 returns only an embedding despite the claimed discrete-token construction. Equation 13 omits a text next-token loss despite describing joint prediction, and the RVQ update, loss weights, selected shallow layer, SLM training duration, inference procedure, and checkpoint selection are unspecified.

Collectively, these evaluation and reproducibility issues make the submission uncompetitive in its current form.

strengths: The core idea is well motivated: making each speech representation correspond to a text token directly addresses the sequence-length mismatch in joint text-speech language modeling.
The proposed system is conceptually simple and useful, combining a frozen ASR encoder, text-conditioned cross-attention aggregation, residual quantization, and lightweight adaptation of a text LLM.

The reported results are promising. TASTE combines a very low token rate with strong reconstruction metrics, while the 1B TASLM obtains competitive continuation quality and particularly strong StoryCloze performance relative to the listed SLMs.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering reconstruction, continuation, acoustic and semantic selection, spoken QA, human judgments, additive-noise robustness, and several architectural and ASR ablations.
weaknesses: The central comparisons are not fully controlled. TASTE reconstructs using an explicit transcript and a global speaker embedding, whereas most codec baselines reconstruct from their transmitted codes alone. Bitrate accounting for all side information is insufficiently documented, and the speaker embedding is never ablated; consequently, the claimed compression and paralinguistic-information advantages cannot be cleanly attributed to TASTE tokens.

The downstream evidence does not isolate text alignment as the cause of the gains. Competing SLMs differ in training data, backbone, model size, and decoding scheme, while the only same-training S3 baseline is poorly specified and appears severely disadvantaged by its length mismatch. Missing controls include uniform or learned pooling at the same token rate, forced-aligned tokens, and matched-compute text-only or transcript-plus-LLM systems.

Because every speech input is explicitly transcribed and the transcript is supplied to the model, strong StoryCloze and spoken-QA results may primarily measure the text LLM and ASR pipeline. Zeroed, shuffled, or removed speech embeddings are needed to establish what acoustic information contributes beyond the transcript.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Broad preservation of paralinguistic information is inferred mainly from duration, speaker similarity, and one qualitative editing example; speaker identity is confounded by the separate speaker embedding, and SALMON results are weak on environmental attributes. The editing claim lacks quantitative comparisons or a listening study.

The human evaluation uses only 20 samples per method, omits confidence intervals, significance tests, rater-quality controls, and important protocol details, and conducts MUSHRA without an anchor. Reported continuation differences such as 4.16 versus 4.00 are small relative to the stated score variability. GPT-4o evaluation also lacks a model version, decoding settings, repeated judgments, and uncertainty analysis.

Technical and reproducibility details are incomplete. The paper omits essential architecture specifications, modality-injection details, loss weights, quantizer optimization details, SLM training duration, inference settings, and training-run variance. The promised code/model URL is blank, and the discrete-token handling after word-level averaging is unclear.

Equation 7 is mathematically inconsistent with the stated Gaussian parameterization: after sampling with standard deviation sigma, the Gaussian KL term should contain sigma squared rather than sigma. The claimed need for a straight-through estimator is also unexplained, leaving uncertainty about the implemented continuous-embedding objective.

Generalization is demonstrated mainly on English and LibriSpeech-derived evaluation data despite roughly 40,600 hours of training. The additive-white-noise experiment also rewards a transcript-conditioned system for denoising rather than fairly measuring reconstruction of the noisy signal. Broader accents, spontaneous speech, real noise, non-lexical events, and unseen domains remain untested.
